learningObjective: Explain why distributed evaluation must sum each shard's TP, FP, TN, and FN counts before computing F1 rather than averaging shard-level F1 values.
mediumRationale: A deterministic two-panel SVG is the smallest medium that can align two shard states with their elementwise sum and then contrast the correct global F1 with the incorrect average of nonlinear shard metrics. Fixed positions preserve the count correspondence and arithmetic without runtime code.

pages.insight: The classification-loss slide establishes probability outputs and numerical handling before evaluation, but does not address streaming state or distributed aggregation.
The neighboring surrogate-loss slide distinguishes several training objectives; it provides context for why training loss and reported classification metrics are separate concerns.
The classification-metrics slide defines precision, recall, F-score, TPR, and FPR from TP, FP, TN, and FN and explicitly shows that scaling negative counts can cancel inside FPR.
The worked binary-evaluation slide uses a 90-negative, 10-positive dataset to derive accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 and sweeps a threshold, but it assumes one in-memory dataset.
The following calibration slide bins predictions and computes a weighted average, illustrating another metric that needs retained bin statistics rather than the four fixed-threshold counts.
The next slide is the activation-functions section divider, confirming that the classification evaluation neighborhood ends at page 39.

deckReview.notes: The complete 214-page local deck was text-indexed for confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, classification metrics, streaming, distributed, merge, shard, worker, sufficient statistics, and aggregation. Pages 35-40 were extracted as the complete classification-loss and evaluation neighborhood, and pages 36-39 were rendered for visual inspection. Pages 37-38 supply the relevant fixed-threshold count formulas, while no slide discusses bounded-memory accumulation, worker merges, or the invalidity of averaging shard F1. Page 39's calibration bins reinforce that different metrics require different retained state. No deck image, example values, wording, or layout is reused.

sourceReview.notes: The hardest prose-only mental model is that mergeability belongs to the retained state, not automatically to the reported scalar. For a fixed threshold, each observation contributes to exactly one of TP, FP, TN, or FN, so disjoint shard vectors add componentwise and in any order. F1 is a ratio of those totals and is nonlinear, so equal-weight averaging of shard F1 values generally changes the estimand. The original example uses shard A (TP=1, FP=0, TN=9, FN=0) and shard B (TP=1, FP=9, TN=1, FN=9). Their F1 values are 1.00 and 0.10, whose mean is 0.55. The merged state is TP=2, FP=9, TN=10, FN=9, yielding global F1 = 4/(4+9+9) = 4/22, approximately 0.18.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, text-indexed all 214 deck pages and visually inspected the full classification-evaluation neighborhood, then checked official scikit-learn count and F1 definitions plus TorchMetrics distributed-state guidance before selecting an original merge counterexample.

implementation.accessibility: Each SVG panel has a linked title and complete description listing all shard counts and both F1 results. Count names, plus and equals signs, ordered rows, a crossed-out averaging path, and explicit CORRECT and WRONG labels carry the distinction without color. The established two-panel primitive stacks below 640 CSS pixels; each compact 300-unit viewBox has no minimum width and uses short labels for readability at 390 CSS pixels. Existing theme variables preserve dark-mode contrast, and shared print tokens produce a light high-contrast figure that stays together.
